Field studies of the White-eared solitaire (Entomodestes leucotis) in the montane cloud forests of the eastern Andes have provided initial metabolic benchmarks for this elusive thrush. Basal oxygen consumption, measured via flow-through respirometry on resting, post-absorptive adults under thermoneutral conditions, averaged 47.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 47.27 milliliters of oxygen per hour] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. These measurements were conducted at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], reflecting the warm, humid microclimate of the understory where these birds typically forage. This metabolic rate is broadly consistent with values predicted for a tropical passerine of its body size, though slightly lower than the typical allometric expectation, suggesting that Entomodestes leucotis is capable of striking a delicate balance between energetic expenditure and thermoregulatory demands in its densely vegetated habitat. Continued sampling across the species elevational range may reveal clinal variation in thermoregulatory physiology, particularly along gradients of temperature and humidity that differ substantially between lower and upper montane forest zones.

Reproductive timing in the White-eared solitaire appears tightly linked to thermal conditions during the breeding season. Females construct cup nests in dense understory vegetation and lay a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], with a maximum reproductive output of approximately one offspring per clutch [N_R_i = approximately one offspring per clutch]. This low annual fecundity, derived from the combination of clutch size and frequency, is characteristic of many tropical montane passerines that invest heavily in parental care. The estimate is based on comparative data from the closely related Turdus eremita, given the paucity of direct long-term nesting observations for Entomodestes leucotis. At the typical brooding temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the energy demands of the nestlings are substantial, requiring frequent provisioning by both adults to sustain growth. The daily reproductive rate implied by these figures is approximately 3 offspring per year [Ri = approximately 3 offspring per year], accounting for the observed clutch frequency.

Neonatal body mass in the White-eared solitaire is remarkably low for a bird of its ultimate adult size. Hatchlings emerge from the egg weighing just 4.3 grams [Wwb = 4.3 grams], a value that is consistent with the altricial developmental mode typical of most passerines. This initial mass stands in stark contrast to the ultimate wet weight attained by adult females, which reaches 61.7 grams [Wwi = 61.7 grams], representing a nearly fifteen-fold increase over the course of the nestling and fledgling periods. The disparity between birth mass and adult mass underscores the intense growth demands placed on provisioning parents during the brief montane breeding season. Data for neonatal mass are extrapolated from measurements on Turdus eremita, a congener with similar reproductive ecology, as direct handling of hatchlings in the field has been limited. This altricial strategy, coupled with the species frugivorous diet, imposes a high energetic cost on the breeding pair, which must gather sufficient food to support both their own metabolism and that of the rapidly growing chicks.

The incubation period and early developmental milestones of the White-eared solitaire are shaped by the thermal environment of the nest. Eggs maintained at a mean incubation temperature of 39 °C [T = 39 °C] hatch after approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days], a duration comparable to that of other high-elevation thrushes, which suggests a degree of evolutionary convergence in developmental rates under similar thermal regimes. Upon hatching, the altricial nestlings are entirely dependent on parental brooding to maintain core body temperature. Fledging, defined as the age at which the chick achieves sustained flight and leaves the nest, occurs at 20 days after hatching [tx = 20 days after hatching], a relatively brief nestling period that is likely an adaptation to reduce predation risk in the open understory at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid developmental pace is facilitated by the high ambient temperatures in the nest microclimate, which average 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] during the active brooding phase. The fledging estimate is informed by comparative data from Turdus eremita and provides a baseline for understanding post-hatching energetics in denizens of the cloud forest.

Longevity and the timing of reproductive maturation in the White-eared solitaire reflect a slow life-history strategy typical of tropical montane birds. Maximum recorded lifespan in the wild is estimated at 11.7 years [am = 11.7 years], based on mark-recapture data and observations of banded individuals at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a delayed onset of reproductive activity. First breeding occurs at 1.5 years since birth [tR = 1.5 years since birth], while the attainment of puberty, or sexual maturity, occurs earlier at 60 days after birth [tp = 60 days after birth] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The prolonged period between sexual maturation and first reproduction is likely tied to the challenges of territory acquisition in dense montane forests and the need to achieve a sufficient body condition to sustain a clutch. Both timing events are recorded at the typical active metabolic temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], underscoring the influence of thermal conditions on the species phenological schedule.
